newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S., S.Korea hail North's peace talks acceptance.
newsitem.headline: U.S., S.Korea hail North's peace talks acceptance.

text.p: South Korea and the United States on Tuesday hailed North Korea's acceptance of four-nation peace talks but immediately braced themselves for a long process of negotiations before any major breakthrough.
"The government of the Republic of Korea welcomes that
the DPRK (North Korea) ... has accepted the proposal for the four-party talks," Seoul Foreign Ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said in a statement.

Communist North Korea on Monday formally agreed to a meeting on August 5 of senior officials from the two Koreas, the United States and China to set an agenda and other procedural details for peace talks.
"We're very pleased with this agreement and we look forward to having this go forward," Deputy U.S. National Security Adviser James Steinberg said in Hong Kong.
Steinberg is accompanying Secretary of State Madeleine Albright at ceremonies in Hong Kong marking the transfer of the territory from British to Chinese control.

U.S. and South Korean officials said engagement by reclusive Pyongyang in serious negotiations to reduce tensions on the Korean peninsula would greatly contribute to peace and security in northeast Asia.
But they cautioned against expectations of quick results.

"The four-party talks proposal intends to initiate the process of establishing a permanent peace on the Korean peninsula, including replacement of the current armistice agreement with a new regime," Lee said.
The 1953 ceasefire pact ended fighting but did not technically end the three-year Korean War, which pitted the North, backed by China, against the South, supported by the U.S.-led United Nations.

Lee told Reuters the troubled North would probably seek concessions but Washington and Seoul were firm in their stand that large-scale food aid and other economic assistance would only be discussed during the peace talks "as part of tension-reduction and confidence-building measures".

"Our purpose is to have peace but we don't expect to achieve our goal in a short span of time," he said. "It is important to keep North Korea engaged in dialogue and take gradual steps to build up confidence."
Steinberg told reporters in Hong Kong that getting the Stalinist North to the bargaining table had been a lengthy process with many false starts.

"But we take it one step at a time because it's been something that we've recognised all along ... is (a) difficult road to go forward and we hope finally this will represent a serious engagement on the four-party process," he said.
The North, threatened by famine and with its economy in ruins, has previously linked its participation to a specific commitment on food aid and an end to U.S. trade sanctions.

Since U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam proposed the four-nation talks in April 1996, the North and South have held numerous working-level meetings and three rounds of negotiations at deputy minister-level before Pyongyang agreed to the August "preparatory talks".
"I would not be surprised if the North introduces other stages before holding the main talks," a Seoul official said.
